title: Report on Studying Abroad at Johns Hopkins University
paragraphs: From March 2011 I did a clerkship at Johns Hopkins Hospital for about three months. Now, as I begin to write this account on the plane home, I feel keenly that this long and memorable experience is at last about to end. Remembering the days I worked hard for this study abroad, I feel a little wistful. I intend to finish writing this report here, so that when I get off this plane I can make a clean mental switch and head toward my next goal.

Looking back, so many things cross my mind that there is no end to listing them: the battle with English and medicine before departure, the various difficulties and walls during the clerkships, the sense of accomplishment I tasted in overcoming them, the many people I was able to meet thanks to studying abroad, and happy memories with my fellow students. I now feel a great sense of accomplishment and gratitude at having spent such wonderful time, which can truly be called the culmination of my university life.

In the first month I did my clerkship in anesthesiology. In anesthesiology, I worked under one resident, learning while helping with that resident's work. Basically it was mostly observation, with the rest being odd jobs, but in the operations, as in the clinical clerkships in Japan, I was actually allowed to do various procedures, from IV, A-line and tracheal intubation to ventilation management and blood pressure management. At first I could not catch the instructions well and even had trouble fetching drugs and equipment, but gradually I learned the flow of the work and felt I was slowly becoming able to function as a member of staff, which was a lot of fun. In addition, I was able to have a truly fulfilling clerkship, such as experiencing night duty twice and being allowed to visit, over two days, the lab of a professor I had been in an operation with. Also, being able to observe cutting-edge operations in various fields every day was very good in that respect too.

In the second month I did my clerkship in hematology. In hematology the schedule began with the morning ward rounds every day, conferences and consults at midday, and in the evening consult rounds and a short lecture by the attending. In the hematology clerkship I struggled quite a lot, both in language and in knowledge. At first I was not given much work and mostly just observed, but with the cooperation of the local student who started the clerkship with me, I was gradually assigned consults and ward patients. It was a clerkship in which I built up a lot of knowledge through conferences and lectures and also gained practical experience, but above all, being able to do the clerkship together with this student for one month was a great stimulus for me.

My last clerkship, in the third month, was in emergency and critical care. In the daily shifts, I was entrusted with two or three patients on average, took the history and examined them, thought out the assessment and plan, presented to the resident in charge, received feedback, and went to see the patient again together with the resident. Because both knowledge and the English I used led directly to ability through experience, I was able to do the clerkship feeling myself grow every day. In addition, I attended lectures and clinical sessions with the local students and rode in ambulances. At the end of the clerkship I also gave a case presentation using PowerPoint. In addition, although not many in number, I also experienced procedures such as IV, blood gases and suturing, and it was a month in which I truly learned many things.

In my time outside the clerkships, I visited doctors who are active in the United States and heard all sorts of stories, traveled around the United States with my fellow exchange students, visited the places where my friends were studying, and played with other exchange students, so there was not a single day that was not fulfilling.

Although it was a short period of three months, it became a truly intense, challenging and fulfilling experience. I would like to sincerely thank everyone who supported my study abroad: my fellow exchange students, the many friends I met at my host institution and in Japan, the professors, and the professors and staff of the International Exchange Office. And I would like to close this report praying that many juniors will take up the challenge of this wonderful experience in the future.
